Anthropology books
recommended by anthropologists
Last updated: September 03, 2026
Anthropology is a field of study of humans, combining insights from psychology, sociology, economics, archaeology and ethnology. Anthropologists may be focused on cultural traditions, social behaviours, or large-scale patterns of behaviour. When we spoke to Oxford University's Professor Ruben Andersson about the best political anthropology books , he offered some reflections on the division between anthropology and some neighbouring fields: "I draw as much inspiration from sociologists as from anthropologists, and I learn a lot from psychologists. In anthropology, we often like to work with how people see the world themselves, the cultural-social world of other people. Many sociologists also work ethnographically, so there’s clear overlap between what we do—that is, following people in their everyday lives. Psychologists, of course, engage with people’s intimate lives on an even more fine-grained scale. So in some ways, we all share methodologies and outlooks, but we all contribute something distinct. In my view, we all get a richer understanding of society, and human sociality, the more we work together."

Anthropologists look for cultural and political currents reflected in everyday behaviours, says Ruben Andersson , the Oxford academic and author of a new book about the contemporary obsession with self-protection, Age of Security. Here, he recommends five anthropology books that have influenced his work and writing—and reflects on the difficulties of recognising patterns in our own thinking.

New techniques have uncovered an enormous amount of information about how humans evolved and new human species continue to pop up on a regular basis. Biological anthropologist Brenna Hassett , author of Growing Up Human , recommends books to learn more about our ancestors and how we became the human beings we are today.
